newsitem.title: GERMANY: German business head says EU jobs pact superfluous.
newsitem.headline: German business head says EU jobs pact superfluous.

text.p: Hans-Olaf Henkel, president of the Federation of German Industry (BDI), said on Tuesday the European Union's planned jobs chapter was superfluous and could be accepted only because it would have no real effect.
Henkel told German Radio he was pleased the EU summit in Amsterdam had agreed to approve the German-inspired stability pact without change because it was needed to ensure a stable single currency.

The jobs chapter, to be added to the Maastricht treaty at France's insistence at the current EU summit in Amsterdam, was simply part of the deal Bonn had to accept to ensure the stability pact was passed, he added.
"I think the German side had played its cards well," Henkel said. "The stability pact is now accepted. We can accept the jobs chapter because it will be without any great effect."
Echoing the German government's position in Amsterdam, the BDI president said he could not approve of any new funds being spent on Europe-wide job-creation schemes.
"Joblessness is not a European problem, it's a problem in many European countries. There are countries that are dealing with unemployment, look at Britain, Ireland and now Portugal.
"There are local and national solutions and we should learn from them and not kick the problem upstairs to Brussels."
Henkel praised new British Prime Minister Tony Blair's focus on more flexible job markets as a useful antidote to what seemed to be a return to more state intervention in France.

"Remember in Europe, we don't have the problem of needing more state intervention, we have too much state intervention," he said. "Successful states are the ones with smaller public sectors. Maybe people on the continent don't understand as much about economic situations as people in Anglo-Saxon countries."
